\chapter{La cita perdida}
\label{ch:es-cita}
\hlchaptermodality{464}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can handle a missed appointment: read the reminder, apologise for not going, say what let me down, and ask for another.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[recordar]{recordar — to remember, and to remind}

\label{lesson:ES-C464-recordar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el corazón} and \textbf{la cita}. The heart is inside the verb that keeps the appointment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: recordar}
\textbf{recordar} — to remember, and also to remind.

\emph{No recuerdo su nombre} — I don't remember his name. \emph{Recuérdame la cita} — remind me about the appointment. \emph{Te recuerdo que mañana es fiesta} — I remind you that tomorrow is a holiday.

One verb, both jobs. Which it is depends on whether somebody else is being told: \emph{recuerdo} alone is remembering, \emph{te recuerdo} is reminding.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: recordar is not acordarse}]
Spanish has a second verb for remembering and the two are near-twins:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{what it takes} \\
\midrule
\emph{recordar algo} & a plain object \\
\emph{acordarse \textbf{de} algo} & \emph{de}, always \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{No recuerdo la dirección} and \emph{no me acuerdo de la dirección} mean the same thing. The difference is grammatical, not semantic: \emph{recordar} takes the thing directly, \emph{acordarse} needs its \textbf{de}, and dropping it is one of the commonest mistakes learners make.

Both are \textbf{o $\to$ ue} verbs: \emph{recuerdo}, \emph{me acuerdo}. The same break you have been tracking since \emph{la rueda}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{recordari}: \textbf{re-}, back, plus \textbf{cor}, \textbf{cordis} — \textbf{the heart}.

To remember is to \textbf{bring back through the heart}, because Latin located memory and thought there rather than in the head. That is the same \emph{cor} inside \textbf{el corazón}, which you have had for many chapters.

The family is everywhere once seen: \textbf{el acuerdo}, an agreement — hearts brought together — and \textbf{recordar}'s English cousin \textbf{record}, which is literally a thing committed to memory. \textbf{Courage} is \emph{cor} too, by way of French, and so is \textbf{concordance}.

So a Spanish speaker asking you to remember something is asking you to run it back past your heart.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I don't remember the appointment
  \item remind me tomorrow
  \item which preposition \emph{acordarse} needs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To remember? (\textbf{Recordar}.) I remember? (\textbf{Recuerdo}.) What is \emph{cor}? (\textbf{The heart} — the same one in \emph{corazón}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el dentista / la dentista]{el dentista / la dentista — the dentist}

\label{lesson:ES-C464-dentista}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el diente} and \textbf{el médico}. Put them together and name the person.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el dentista}
\textbf{el dentista}, \textbf{la dentista} — the dentist.

\emph{Tengo cita con el dentista} — I've got a dentist's appointment. \emph{Voy al dentista} — I'm going to the dentist's.

Note \emph{al dentista} for the place as well as the person: Spanish sends you to the professional, not to the surgery, where English says \textquotedblleft{}to the dentist's\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -ista does not change for gender}]
\textbf{-ista} nouns have one form for both, and only the article moves:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the person} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
dentist & el dentista & la dentista \\
artist & el artista & la artista \\
tourist & el turista & la turista \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{-a} ending misleads, because it looks feminine and is not. \emph{El dentista} is correct and \emph{el dentisto} does not exist.

Compare \emph{el médico / la médica}, which does change. The difference is the ending: \emph{-ista} is invariable, \emph{-o} is not. Learn the ending and the article stops being a guess — the same bargain the noun-making suffixes offered.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{dens}, \textbf{dentem} — \textbf{tooth} — plus the Greek ending \textbf{-istēs}, which names somebody who does a thing.

So \emph{dentista} is a Latin body part with a Greek job-ending welded on, which is how most modern profession words were built: \emph{el periodista}, \emph{el electricista}, \emph{el taxista}. The ending is productive, meaning Spanish still makes new ones.

\emph{Dentem} gives \textbf{el diente}, and English \textbf{dental}, \textbf{dentist} and \textbf{indent} — to cut a tooth-shaped notch. A \textbf{dandelion} is \emph{dent de lion}, a lion's tooth, named for its leaves.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I've got a dentist's appointment
  \item a female dentist, with the right article
  \item why \emph{el dentista} is not a mistake
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The dentist? (\textbf{El dentista} or \textbf{la dentista}.) Does the noun change? (\textbf{No} — only the article.) What is \emph{dentem}? (\textbf{A tooth}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fallar]{fallar — to fail somebody}

\label{lesson:ES-C464-fallar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{falso} and \textbf{estropeado}. One is about truth, one about machines. The verb next covers both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fallar}
\textbf{fallar} — to fail, to go wrong, to let somebody down.

\emph{Me falló el coche} — the car let me down. \emph{Ha fallado el sistema} — the system has gone down. \emph{No me falles} — don't let me down.

\textbf{El fallo} is the noun: a fault, a glitch, and in an exam a wrong answer.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: fallar is not estropearse}]
Both are about things going wrong, and they are not the same:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what happened} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
it stopped working, and stayed that way & \textbf{estropearse} \\
it did not do its job at the moment needed & \textbf{fallar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Se ha estropeado el coche} — it is broken, in the garage. \emph{Me falló el coche} — it let me down, this morning, when I needed it. A car can \emph{fallar} once and be fine afterwards.

That is why \emph{fallar} is the verb for people too. \emph{Me falló} about a friend is a reproach: they were not there when it counted.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{fallere}, to deceive — and that is the same verb inside \textbf{falso}, which you already have.

The move from deceiving to failing runs through disappointment: something that \emph{fails} you has, in effect, misled you about what it would do. Latin \emph{fallere} already carried both, and Spanish kept the pair — \emph{falso} for the lie, \emph{fallar} for the letting-down.

English took it twice as well: \textbf{false} from the participle, and \textbf{fail} through French. \textbf{Fault}, \textbf{fallacy} and \textbf{failure} are all here, and so is \textbf{default}, which is a failing to act.

A second Spanish branch is \textbf{faltar}, to be lacking — \emph{me falta tiempo}, I'm short of time — from the same root by a different road.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the car let me down this morning
  \item don't let me down
  \item which verb fits a washing machine that has stopped for good
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To let somebody down? (\textbf{Fallar}.) The noun? (\textbf{El fallo}.) What did \emph{fallere} mean? (\textbf{To deceive} — the same verb as \emph{falso}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(recordar, el dentista, fallar)]{(recordar, el dentista, fallar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R464-repaso-cita}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: \emph{to remember}, \emph{the dentist}, \emph{to let down}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two bodies and a lie}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new word} & \textbf{what it was built on} \\
\midrule
\textbf{recordar} & \emph{cor}, the heart — the one in \emph{el corazón} \\
\textbf{el dentista} & \emph{dentem}, a tooth — the one in \emph{el diente} \\
\textbf{fallar} & \emph{fallere}, to deceive — the one in \emph{falso} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two body parts and a lie, and all three were already in your vocabulary. By this stage that is the ordinary case rather than a happy accident: a corpus of nine hundred words contains most of the roots the next hundred will need.

\textbf{Recordar} is the one worth keeping. Latin put memory in the \textbf{heart}, not the head, so remembering is running a thing back past it — and English \textbf{record} is the same word, a thing committed to memory.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: endings that fix the article, and one that does not}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{what it settles} \\
\midrule
-ista & \textbf{nothing changes}; only the article moves \\
-o / -a & the noun itself changes: \emph{el médico}, \emph{la médica} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El dentista} looks feminine and is not. That \textbf{-a} is Greek, not the Spanish feminine, which is why the noun stays put and the article does the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item remind me about the dentist
  \item the car let me down
  \item which of the three words has a heart inside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence about an appointment you nearly missed.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(perder la cita) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C464-sintesis-cita}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{recordar} and \textbf{fallar}. The first message does one; the second admits the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Two messages, a day apart. Read both, then answer.

\textbf{1 — de la clínica}

\begin{quote}
Le \textbf{recordamos} su cita con la \textbf{dentista} el jueves a las 10:15. Para anular, llame con 24 horas de antelación.
\end{quote}

\textbf{2 — el jueves por la tarde}

\begin{quote}
Buenas tardes. Siento no haber ido esta mañana; me \textbf{falló} el despertador y no me acordé hasta las once. ¿Puedo pedir otra cita?
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item when the appointment was, and who with
  \item what you must do to cancel, and how far ahead
  \item the two things that went wrong
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
The apology uses \textbf{both} verbs for remembering and they are doing different work. \textbf{Me falló el despertador} — the alarm clock is the subject; it let the writer down. Then \textbf{no me acordé} — \emph{acordarse}, the reflexive one, for the person's own failure to recall. Spanish separates the thing that failed from the person who forgot, and the apology is more honest for it.

\textbf{La dentista}, feminine, so the clinic is naming a particular woman. And \emph{con la dentista}, not \emph{con el dentista} — had the message said \emph{el}, you would know it was a man, since the noun itself never tells you.

\textbf{Siento no haber ido} is the standard apology frame: \emph{sentir} plus a perfect infinitive. Not \emph{siento que no fui}, which a learner reaches for and a Spanish speaker does not.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines: as the clinic, remind somebody of a dental appointment and say how to cancel; then as the patient, apologise for missing it, say what let you down, and ask for another.

Then check yourself: did \emph{fallar} go to the thing and \emph{acordarse} to the person, and did \emph{acordarse} keep its \emph{de}?
\end{tcolorbox}
